tecnicas.observacao: O modelo explica o programa-fonte em poucas frases antes de traduzir (explicação antes do código → raciocinio). Nos experimentos Python-to-X, as explicações são geradas em Python-Java e reutilizadas, após remoção programática de informação específica do alvo.

riscos.descricao: O estudo menciona a possibilidade de a explicação alucinar a semântica do programa a partir dos nomes de variáveis; com código ofuscado, a explicação dependeria mais da sintaxe.

O conjunto TransCoder provavelmente consta dos corpora de treino dos GPTs (o modelo regurgita programas a partir da assinatura); é uma das razões para não avaliá-lo formalmente. O estudo não discute contaminação do MultiPL-C2C/HumanEval.
Aproximar a dificuldade por tradução direta (estratégia select) exige mais computação que gerar uma explicação; não quantificado.

Validade externa: não se sabe se os programas do MultiPL-E representam alvos reais de tradução, nem se as conclusões valem para modelos mais fortes como GPT-4; explicações pouco úteis no cenário few-shot.
Qualidade dos benchmarks: mais de 25% dos exemplos de CodeXGLUE/TransCoder examinados têm erros em programas-gabarito ou testes inadequados.

citacoes.trecho: In this paper we are interested in whether a self-generated natural language explanation z can be used to improve this translation process.

Across three types of explanations and 19 programming languages constructed from the MultiPL-E dataset (Cassano et al., 2022), we find the explanations to be particularly effective in the zero-shot case, improving performance by 12% on average.
We find that Explain-then-Translate improves zero-shot performance consistently in 18 Python-to-X translation directions, but much less so in the few-shot setting.
We analyze our results in 36 different translation directions over different types of explanations.
exp: We ask the model to explain the source program in a few sentences (Fig 1, right).
exp-lbl: We ask the model to explain the source program line by line.
exp-lbl-d: We ask the model to explain the source program line by line in additional detail.
In particular if an individual line is complicated, we ask it to break it down, explain individual fragment of the line, and then summarize the purpose for the entire line.
Please translate the following Python code to R?
Can you explain what this Python program does with a couple of sentences? The goal with the explanation, is so that a reader can easily rewrite the program in R.

When generating explanations, we treat the token sequence \n# as a stopping sequence in order to prevent models from generating target translations (since we condition target program with translated signatures in addition to explanations).

In order to control for inconsistencies caused by the target-language-specific explanations, we re-use the same explanations (from Python-Java) for all Python-to-X translation experiments (Section 3.1).
Before reusing, we also remove any target specific information with programmatic rules so it can be reused across experiments.
We prioritize precision and calculate pass@1 with n = 20, t = 0.2, and top-p= 0.95 following Cassano et al. (2022).

We main report the results from GPT-3.5 (gpt3.5-turbo-0301) in the main paper unless otherwise specified, and defer the results from open source models (CodeGen2-1B, CodeGen2-16B, and Llama2CodeInstruct-34B (Nijkamp et al., 2023; Rozière et al., 2023)) to the appendix.
All completion queries are made to GPT-3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo-3010) between March - June 2023.
You are a helpful and faithful compiler that transpiles Python code to Java code.
You are an helpful AI assistant who understands all programming languages and can translate between them at ease.
Providing explanations improves relative performance by 11.5% on average across 18 target languages.
In the four-shot setting, the average improvement is much less at 1.1%, although some language pairs observe as much as a 10.1% improvement.
The most abstract explanation (exp) performs the worst (best in only 3 out of 18 directions) in the few-shot setting.
Since source languages are different, we do not re-use explanations.
In the four-shot explanation, we use zero-shot generated explanations (3.1).
We speculate that LLMs generally struggle to understand and explain lower-resource PLs; more details may introduce more errors which may compound into the translation phase.
CodeGen2-16B is the only model that does not improve consistently with explanations.
For each explanation type, we generate 20 explanations and 1 program from each explanation (train set).
We use zero-shot explanations for exp (see Sec 3.1) and four-shot for exp-lbl and exp-lbl-d.
With exp, logprob improves upon random by absolute 2.54% (p = 0.055), and frag improves explain-lbl-d upon random baseline by absolute 2.2% (p = 0.033) with simulation.

citacoes.trecho: Both improvements can be reproduced with pass@1, so we include these heuristically selected explanations as two additional rows in Table 1.
With logprob selected exp, we improve or match performance in 15/18 directions, with an average improvement of 1.7% (p < 0.001).
With frag selected exp-lbl-simp, we improve or match performance in 13/18 directions, averaging 0.48% (p = 0.022).
Repeated 100 times to obtain mean and variance.

Qualitatively, we could not distinguish a good explanation from a bad one manually (Apx L.3 and L.4), suggesting that the distinction between “good” and “bad” explanations may be hidden due to stylistic noise (wording, spacing, etc.), or potentially due to chance.
Through Fig 4, we discovered that explanation improves difficult problems (left of x-axis), but could hurt easy problems (right of x-axis).
We found selective explanation to improve performance over direct and exp in 35/36 directions.

We replace the explanation with another program’s explanation randomly (rand-exp), or through retrieval (ret-exp, details in Apx O), or with an empty string (no-exp) to verify if explanations need to be correct/relevant.

Lastly, when models receive completely irrelevant explanations (rand-exp), they are able to recover performance to some extent; but if the explanations are convincingly misleading (ret-exp) performance deterioates.
This is potentially due to the fact that explanations become more reliant on actual syntax of the program, rather than hallucinating on the program semantics from surface variable names.
In Table 5, we observe that when the retrieved one-shot is paired with a wrong target program, the decrease in performance is much more significant than in the fixed-shot setting.

However, on average, self-generated unverified explanations (exp) still outperform one-shot in all directions (fixed-unk by 0.7-4.5%; retrieve-unk by 0.5-2.0%), indicating that NL generations often have higher quality than programs and can serve as a better medium for intermediate reasoning step.
retrieval-bad (Table 5) should be taken lightly since the subset of problems evaluated for bad also likely contains harder problems.
The result indicates mistakes in intermediate PL steps corrupt translation performance more than imperfect NL explanations.
With simple heuristics, we have also demonstrated the potential to improve explanation quality and consequently translation quality.

First, while we focus on the (adapted) MultiPL-E benchmark due to its widespread use, it is unclear whether programs in this benchmark are representative of programs that are targets for code-to-code translation.
Second, while we saw our conclusions to largely hold across GPT-3.5 and other open-source models, it is unclear whether they will hold for more powerful LLMs such as GPT-4.

We also considered into CodeXGLUE (Lu et al., 2021) and TransCoder (Lachaux et al., 2020) for the unit tests evaluations, but initial studies suggested a significant number of examples (more than 25%) contain mistakes in gold programs or inadequate unit tests (see Apx A, B).
One of the other reasons that we do not formally evaluate our methods on TransCoder dataset is because that the TransCoder dataset is very likely to have been included in GPTs’ training corpora.

qualidade.justificativa: A pergunta é explícita: saber se uma explicação autogerada em linguagem natural melhora a tradução de código, em várias linguagens e níveis de recurso.

Os prompts completos (four-shot) estão no Apx C, e a construção do MultiPL-C2C, a métrica, os parâmetros e o pós-processamento estão descritos (§2, Apx E). Porém o «train set» das heurísticas não é definido, os prompts zero-shot completos aparecem só no exemplo da Fig. 1, o prompt one-shot (Tabela 5) não é mostrado, e parte dos exemplos few-shot foi escolhida arbitrariamente e editada à mão.

Linha de base direct executada no mesmo benchmark, métrica e cenário de shots (zero e four-shot), além de ablações (no-exp, rand-exp, ret-exp), comparadores one-shot e baseline random para as heurísticas.

O pass@1 é definido (n = 20, t = 0.2, top-p = 0.95), mas várias análises usam n = 1; os denominadores por linguagem não aparecem na Tabela 1 (só na coluna «total» da Tabela 14, sem definição); e a mesma métrica tem valores diferentes entre tabelas (php em exp four-shot: 81.7 na Tabela 1 × 76.4 na Tabela 9; py-sh e py-rs nas Tabelas 1 × 14).

A seção Limitations discute a representatividade do benchmark, a generalização para GPT-4 e a pouca utilidade no few-shot; há cautelas sobre subconjuntos (nota 11) e acaso (§3.4). Faltam teste estatístico ou variabilidade para os resultados principais da Tabela 1 e a discussão do ajuste dos exemplos few-shot feito na direção Python→Java, que também é avaliada.
